story.title: Small-business software was the first thing SaaS came for and the thing SaaS got wrong.
body: The last decade's answer was a subscription portal, a monthly bill, and the expectation that your business records would live on hardware you had never seen. For a sole-trader electrician, a three-partner law firm, or a patient at a renal unit, that was never a good trade.

The mistake was treating every problem as a cloud problem. Most of them aren't. A tradie needs job folders they can find next Tuesday; a solicitor needs matter files with an audit trail that holds up at a Law Society review; a dialysis patient needs a careful logbook the nephrology team can read when the batteries are fine and when they aren't. None of that needs the documents to leave the office.

Adapdev started from the other end. One development team, a stubborn preference for software that installs on hardware you own, and a shape of engagement where either a product off the shelf fits you, or we build you something that does. Two products so far — ADMS, in use today; the Home Dialysis Tracker, in development for 2027 — and a bespoke practice behind them that keeps the catalogue honest.
That is the whole idea. Everything we ship exists to be the easiest way to do the thing you came to it to do, and the hardest way to accidentally lose it.

rules.title: A few things we will not do

items.text: No cloud lock-in. Your database is on your hardware. If you stop paying Adapdev, the software keeps running and your files stay yours.

texture.alt: Folded fabric lit from the side

items.text: No per-seat multiplier. One-off licence for products, fixed-price scope for bespoke work. Adding a teammate doesn't restart the invoice.
No tier-one support queue. The developer who shipped the release is the person who answers the bug report.
No account you didn't create. There is no sign-up screen on anything we ship, no mandatory telemetry, no email list you got added to.
